newsitem.title: USA: Russia bond may open issue floodgates - US investors.
newsitem.headline: Russia bond may open issue floodgates - US investors.

text.p: Russia first foray since Czarist times into the global debt markets should solidify the country's recovery and light a path for future bond issuance, U.S. investors said Monday.

U.S. portfolio managers said Russia's Eurobond issue, which is on roadshow this week, could lead to the Russian government and corporatations raising $2.0 billion to $5.0 billion on the global capital markets next year.

"There's a lot of money to be raised by Russian entities, both government and private," Nikhil Dhaon, vice president at Morgan Stanley Asset Management. "I think we will see a lot of Russian paper come to market, both in equity and debt."
For weeks, the emerging debt market has been captivated by Russia's inaugural Eurobond, for which investors will likely scramble at 300-350 basis points over U.S. Treasuries.

"I'm sure it's going to be very successful," one U.S. mutual fund analyst said of the Eurobond. "The Russians are going to be ready come out with more paper next year, around the time they finish restructuring the Vnesh loans."

The Eurobond, likely to be a five-year issue, should benefit Russian companies that have clean balance sheets and sound products, particularly dollar-based entities and commodity exporters, opening a way to the dollar debt market.

The Russian government must decide whether to push for a tight spread, which could aid future corporate issuers, or delight international investors by issuing at a wide spread that could tighten in the secondary trading.
"If I were the Russians I would be pushing for a hard, tight spread," one U.S. investor said.

A warm reception to the Eurobond would put the finishing touches to a tumultuous year in which the country addressed great uncertainties: a presidential election, negotiations with the International Monetary Fund, and the soon-to-be- completed restructuring of Vneshekonombank loans.

Russia's debt assets will likely perform well next year, although not at the magnificent level of 1996, when the country's debt prices have brought returns of about 120 percent year-to-date, U.S. investors said.

"I am very optimistic on Russia for the foreseeable future," said Eduardo Cortes, portfolio manager at JP Morgan Asset Management. "With the Eurobond, you get an attractive credit in a country on a significant path of improvement."
Cortes added there would be bumps down the road, which would be difficult to foresee but would provide significant opportunities to buy and sell financial assets.
Prospects for Russian debt aside, analysts said they would be looking for improvements in the real economy to solidify the economic liberalization.
The Eurobond would also probably force the emerging market bond indices to revise their weightings.
"In this age of yield hunger and need for diversification, Russia is going to have a big weighting in the market," one portfolio manager said.
